notes.definition: A distance–time graph shows how the distance travelled by an object moving in a straight line changes with time. The gradient (slope) of a distance–time graph equals the speed of the object.
explanation: When an object moves along a straight line, its motion can be shown on a distance–time graph, with time on the horizontal axis and distance on the vertical axis. The shape of the line tells you how the object is moving. A horizontal line means the distance is not changing, so the object is stationary. A straight sloping line means equal distances are covered in equal times, so the object is moving at a constant speed.

The gradient of a distance–time graph is equal to the speed. To find it, pick two points on a straight section, far apart, and calculate gradient = change in distance ÷ change in time ("rise over run"). For example, if the distance increases from 20 m to 80 m between 4 s and 16 s, the speed is (80 − 20) ÷ (16 − 4) = 60 ÷ 12 = 5 m/s. A steeper line means a greater speed. A line sloping downwards (on a graph of distance from a fixed point) shows the object moving back towards its starting point.

If the line is curved, the speed is changing. A curve that gets steeper shows the object speeding up (accelerating). A curve that gets less steep shows the object slowing down (decelerating). You can calculate the average speed over any interval as total distance ÷ total time, using the values read from the graph.

(Higher) For an accelerating object the speed at a particular instant can be found by drawing a tangent to the curve at that time. A tangent is a straight line that just touches the curve at that point, with the same slope as the curve there. Make the tangent long, then draw a large right-angled triangle on it and calculate its gradient: speed = change in distance ÷ change in time for the triangle.

You should be able to draw a distance–time graph from measurements. Put time (the independent variable) on the x-axis and distance on the y-axis, choose scales that use most of the grid, label axes with quantities and units, plot points accurately and draw a line of best fit (straight or a smooth curve). You should also be able to translate between graphs and numbers: read off distances and times, calculate speeds from gradients, and sketch a graph from a description of a journey.
keyFacts: On a distance–time graph, time goes on the x-axis and distance on the y-axis.
Gradient of a distance–time graph = speed.
Gradient = change in distance ÷ change in time.
Curve getting steeper: accelerating; curve getting less steep: decelerating.
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time, read from the graph.
(Higher) Speed at an instant on a curved graph = gradient of the tangent at that time.

keyTerms.definition: A graph of distance travelled (y-axis) against time (x-axis) for an object moving in a straight line.
The steepness of a line: change in y-value ÷ change in x-value. On a distance–time graph it gives speed.
A straight line that touches a curve at one point and has the same gradient as the curve at that point.
Not moving: the distance does not change with time, so the line is horizontal.
Equal distances travelled in equal times; shown by a straight, sloping line.
A straight line or smooth curve drawn through or close to plotted points to show the trend.

workedExamples.title: Speed from a straight section
workedExamples.question: A distance–time graph for a jogger is a straight line from (0 s, 0 m) to (50 s, 150 m). Calculate her speed.
steps: Speed = gradient = change in distance ÷ change in time.
Change in distance = 150 − 0 = 150 m; change in time = 50 − 0 = 50 s.

workedExamples.title: Reading a multi-stage journey
workedExamples.question: The graph in Diagram 1 shows a cyclist's journey: 0 to 100 m in the first 20 s, no change from 20 s to 40 s, then 100 m to 200 m from 40 s to 50 s. Calculate the speed in each stage and the average speed.
steps: Stage B: horizontal line, so the speed is 0 m/s (stationary for 20 s).
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time = 200 ÷ 50 = 4 m/s.

workedExamples.title: (Higher) Tangent to a curve
workedExamples.question: A car accelerates from rest. Its distance–time graph is a curve. A tangent drawn at t = 6 s passes through (3 s, 0 m) and (10 s, 42 m). Calculate the speed of the car at 6 s.
steps: The speed at an instant is the gradient of the tangent at that time.
Change in distance = 42 − 0 = 42 m; change in time = 10 − 3 = 7 s.

workedExamples.title: Converting units from a graph
workedExamples.question: A distance–time graph for a walker shows 1.8 km travelled in 20 minutes at a constant speed. Calculate the speed in m/s.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a horizontal line on a distance–time graph means the object is moving at a constant speed.
misconceptions.right: In fact a horizontal line means the distance is not changing, so the object is stationary. Constant speed is a straight sloping line.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often read the speed straight off the y-axis of a distance–time graph.
misconceptions.right: In fact the y-axis shows distance. Speed is the gradient: change in distance ÷ change in time.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a steep line means the object has travelled a long way.
misconceptions.right: In fact steepness shows speed, not total distance. A short, steep section means fast motion over a short time.

misconceptions.wrong: (Higher) Students often find the speed at an instant on a curve by dividing the distance at that point by the time.
misconceptions.right: In fact distance ÷ time gives the average speed from the start. The instantaneous speed is the gradient of the tangent at that point.

realWorld: Running and cycling apps plot distance against time; steeper sections show where you were moving fastest.
Train timetables can be turned into distance–time graphs, where flat sections show the train stopped at stations.
Police and accident investigators use distance–time data from dashcams to work out vehicle speeds.
Data loggers with motion sensors produce distance–time graphs directly in school experiments.
higherTier: If an object is accelerating, its speed at any particular time is found by drawing a tangent to the distance–time graph at that time and measuring the gradient of the tangent.
examTips: When calculating a gradient, use a large triangle and read values carefully from the grid. Show the numbers you read off, as method marks are awarded for them.
Check the axis units: if time is in minutes or distance in km, convert to s and m to get m/s.
Describe each section of a graph in words: "horizontal so stationary", "straight slope so constant speed", "steeper so faster".
(Higher) Draw tangents with a ruler, touching the curve at one point only, and extend them well beyond the point so the gradient triangle is large.
When plotting a graph, label both axes with quantity and unit, use more than half the grid, and draw a single smooth line of best fit.
summary: Distance–time graphs show distance travelled against time for straight-line motion.
Gradient = speed = change in distance ÷ change in time.
Horizontal = stationary; straight slope = constant speed; steeper = faster.
Curves show changing speed: getting steeper = accelerating.
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.
(Higher) Instantaneous speed = gradient of a tangent to the curve.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows the distance–time graph for a ball rolling across a floor.
What is happening to the ball?
options: It is moving at constant speed
markScheme: 1 mark: D
questions.explanation: A decreasing gradient means a decreasing speed: the ball is decelerating, for example due to friction.

questions.question:
A student plots a distance–time graph for a toy car.
Which variable should the student plot on the x-axis?
markScheme: 1 mark: A
questions.explanation: Time is the independent variable, so it is plotted on the horizontal (x) axis. Distance goes on the y-axis.

questions.question:
The distance–time graph for a runner is curved.
How should you find the speed of the runner at exactly t = 8 s?
options: Divide the distance at 8 s by 8 s
Draw a tangent at 8 s and find its gradient
Find the area under the graph up to 8 s
Read the value on the y-axis at 8 s
markScheme: 1 mark: B
questions.explanation: On a curve, the instantaneous speed is the gradient of the tangent. A gives the average speed from the start; C has no meaning for a distance–time graph; D gives the distance, not the speed.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a distance–time graph for an object. A tangent has been drawn to the curve at t = 4 s.
What is the speed of the object at t = 4 s?
markScheme: 1 mark: A
questions.explanation: Gradient of tangent = (20 − 0) ÷ (10 − 2) = 20 ÷ 8 = 2.5 m/s. 2.0 m/s comes from 20 ÷ 10 and 5.0 m/s from 20 ÷ 4.

questions.question:
Table 1 gives information about the journey of a train.
Calculate the average speed of the train for the whole journey.
Give your answer in m/s.
markScheme: 1 mark: total distance 20 000 m and total time 12 min = 720 s
questions.explanation: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time, including the 2 minutes stopped: 20 000 ÷ 720 = 27.8 m/s.

questions.question:
A student walks at a constant speed of 1.4 m/s. Her distance–time graph starts at the origin.
Calculate the distance shown on the graph at t = 45 s.
markScheme: 1 mark: s = v t = 1.4 × 45
1 mark: 63 m
questions.explanation: For a straight line through the origin, distance = speed × time = 1.4 × 45 = 63 m.

markScheme: 1 mark: find the gradient of the line
1 mark: gradient = change in distance ÷ change in time (using two points on the line)
questions.explanation: Speed is the gradient of a distance–time graph.

questions.question: Describe the motion shown by a distance–time graph that is a curve getting steeper.
markScheme: 1 mark: gradient increases
1 mark: so the speed is increasing / the object is accelerating
questions.explanation: The gradient is the speed, so an increasing gradient means increasing speed.

questions.question:
A student times a toy car. Table 1 shows the results.
Describe the shape of the distance–time graph for the toy car.
Calculate the speed of the toy car.
markScheme: 1 mark: straight line through the origin
1 mark: so constant speed
1 mark: speed = 2.4 ÷ 6 = 0.4 m/s
questions.explanation: Equal distances (0.8 m) in equal times (2 s) means a constant speed of 0.4 m/s.

questions.question: Give two things a student should do when drawing a distance–time graph from measurements.
acceptedAnswers: use more than half the grid
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: time on x-axis and distance on y-axis; label axes with quantity and unit; choose a scale using more than half the grid; plot points accurately; draw a line of best fit (straight or smooth curve)
questions.explanation: Good graph-drawing technique is assessed in AQA exams.

questions.question: Explain how to use a distance–time graph to find the speed of an accelerating car at a time of 5 s.
markScheme: 1 mark: draw a tangent to the curve at t = 5 s
1 mark: draw a large right-angled triangle on the tangent
1 mark: speed = change in distance ÷ change in time for the triangle (gradient of the tangent)
questions.explanation: Because the car is accelerating, the graph is curved, so only the tangent gives the speed at one instant.

questions.question:
A student calculates the speed of an accelerating object at 10 s by dividing the distance at 10 s by 10 s.
Explain why this does not give the speed of the object at 10 s.
markScheme: 1 mark: this gives the average speed from 0 to 10 s
1 mark: the speed at 10 s is the gradient of a tangent at 10 s (it is greater than the average because the object is accelerating)
questions.explanation: Distance ÷ time from the origin is an average; instantaneous speed needs a tangent.

questions.question:
A girl walks to a bus stop at a constant speed. She waits at the bus stop. She then travels on a bus at a higher constant speed in the same direction.
Sketch the distance–time graph for this journey and describe each section of the graph.
markScheme: Indicative content:
Axes: time on x-axis, distance on y-axis
First section: straight line with a shallow positive gradient (walking at constant speed)
Second section: horizontal line (stationary while waiting)
Third section: straight line with a steeper positive gradient (bus faster)
Gradient represents speed so steeper means faster
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): all three sections correctly described with reference to gradient
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two sections correctly described
0 marks: no relevant content
questions.explanation: Each stage of motion has a characteristic shape: shallow slope, flat, steeper slope.

questions.question:
A student uses a motion sensor to record the distance of a trolley from a starting line. The trolley is released from rest and rolls down a ramp. The distance–time graph is a curve that gets steeper.
Explain what the graph shows about the motion of the trolley.
Describe how the student could use the graph to find:
• the average speed over the first 2 seconds
• the speed of the trolley at exactly 2 seconds.
Explain why the two values are different.
markScheme: Indicative content:
Curve getting steeper shows the gradient increasing, so the speed increases: the trolley is accelerating
(a) read distance at 2 s from the graph; average speed = distance ÷ 2 s
(b) draw a tangent to the curve at t = 2 s with a ruler
Draw a large triangle on the tangent; speed = change in distance ÷ change in time
The instantaneous speed at 2 s is greater than the average over 0 to 2 s
because the trolley started from rest and was speeding up, so it was slower for most of the 2 s
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): correct interpretation, both methods described clearly, and a correct explanation of the difference
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct interpretation and one method, or both methods without explanation
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example the trolley is speeding up
0 marks: no relevant content
questions.explanation: This question tests the difference between average speed (total distance ÷ total time) and instantaneous speed (tangent gradient, Higher).
